sweep_summary: Sukuma (suku1261) is not in the catalog. Of the four title-keyword items, only Roberts 1992 was readable (already held by the project, re-read): it is a tone-shift paper with no stress statement. The other three could not be obtained open: Matondo 2003 UCLA dissertation (ProQuest/UMI only; eScholarship, UCLA pages, Google Books, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar all empty or unreachable), Philippson 1991 Paris 5 thesis (theses.fr: not accessible online; abstract read via the theses.fr API -- a ~30-language typology of tone vs penultimate demarcative accent, Sukuma not named in the abstract; an open-record condensed version, Philippson 1998 Faits de langues DOI 10.3406/flang.1998.1225, sits behind Persée's page-image viewer), and Idsardi & Purnell 1995 'Sukuma accent' (CLS 31, print only; not on either author's web page; 'accent' there is most likely the abstract metrical accent used to derive the two-syllable H shift). All three are 'unclear' at medium priority. The best first-hand prominence statement actually read is Herrmann 1898 (MSOS 1), verified on page images: default penultimate 'Accent' with antepenultimate in -ga stems and some present/future forms, plus emphatic final syllables -- a pre-tonal impressionistic description; all modern sources held by the project treat Sukuma as tonal with no word-stress statement. search addendum appended to (UTC stamp script-emitted); no new files downloaded this search of works with stress in the title (the Persée PDF attempt could not be reached by automated download and was deleted). searches were done via DuckDuckGo/Bing downloads and open APIs.

new_statements.translation: Besides this simple stem every verb has another one, formed by attaching the syllable -ga, e.g. -túlaga, -ímbaga, -ógaga, where the accent (Ton) stays on the formerly penultimate syllable, i.e. now rests on the antepenult. [p.178] || 5. The last syllable of words is mostly thrust out with vehemence, whereby the final vowel becomes short. 6. The accentuation (Betonung) is very clear and emphatic, as if one wanted to convince the addressee of the truth of the words (as in Kigogo). [p.146] || Not all verbs take the accent on the antepenultimate syllable in this form [Present 1], as ndītula does, but only those where it is convenient to pronounce. [p.179]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pre-tonal 1898 description: 'Ton/Accent' (perceived prominence, acute-marked throughout the word lists) sits on the penultimate syllable of the simple verb stem (ku-túla, kw-ímba, k-óga) and is a property of the stem: it stays on that syllable when the suffix -ga is added, so it then falls on the word antepenult (-túlaga; n-alu-túlaga). In some tense forms (Present 1 with prefix di/li, Future) the accent goes to the third-from-last syllable of the word (n-dī-tula; 'Hier kann der Accent auch auf die 3. letzte Silbe kommen'), but 'not all verbs' do this. With the noun suffix -ki the accent falls on the last syllable of the noun (múnhúki, ntíki) — i.e. the word penult. Nouns in the lists are marked mostly penult but not uniformly (múnhu, ndáva, ssúdyi, múmbi, nugúti; bañhu, kado unmarked). Taken together the placement is morphologically anchored and not a single fixed word position; modern work (Richardson 1959, Batibo 1976/1985/1991, Goldsmith 1985, Sietsema 1989, Roberts 1992, Matondo 2003/2006) analyses Sukuma prominence purely as lexical/grammatical H tone with two-syllable rightward shift, so Herrmann's 'Accent' almost certainly records tone (H) rather than stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Present 1 and Future forms may shift the accent to the antepenult 'wie beim 1. Praesens', 'aber nur die, bei denen es sich bequem aussprechen lässt' (pp.179-180); interrogative suffix -ki attracts accent to the noun's final syllable (p.174); final syllable of words 'mit Vehemenz herausgestossen', final vowel shortened (p.146).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (verb stem, inflected verb forms, noun + enclitic -ki), citation forms in a missionary/officer grammar; author explicitly notes he could not always identify sounds reliably and does not recognise tone. No modern opened source (Batibo 1991, Roberts 1992, Sietsema 1989, Goldsmith 1990, Matondo 2006, Luhende 2018) makes any statement about Sukuma word stress or penultimate lengthening; Batibo 1991 pp.21-22 only says that the stress of loanwords' source languages 'was interpreted as a high tone in penultimate or final syllable' / 'has surfaced on a short, usually penultimate vowel'; Luhende 2018 sec. 2.2.5: 'Sukuma is a tonal language.. three basic tones.. H, L, FR'.
new_statements.identity_note: Herrmann 1898 describes explicitly 'der Dialekt der am Speke-Golf und Smith-Sund gelegenen nordwestlichen Stämme' (north-western Sukuma, Lake Victoria shore; data gathered 1893 and 1897 via Swahili-speaking informants) — Glottolog has no matching dialect node; nearest are the suku1261 children gwee1241 'Gwe' (Kigwe = Sukuma per Guthrie) and kiya1238 'Kiya' (Jinakiiya). Modern tone descriptions cover other dialects: Richardson 1959/1971 (data reused by Goldsmith 1985, Sietsema 1989, Roberts 1992) and Batibo 1976/1985 ('a different dialect', Sietsema p.240; Batibo's Kemunasukuma); Masele 2000/2001 and Matondo 2003 work on Jinakiiya (kiya1238).

new_statements.reading: A pre-tonal (1898) description of the north-western (Speke Gulf / Smith Sound) dialect: perceived word prominence ('Accent', marked with acutes throughout the wordlists) is by default on the penultimate syllable, staying in place (hence antepenultimate) when the -ga stem extension is added, with antepenultimate accent also in certain Praesens 1 and future forms, and a final-syllable emphasis with shortening. Herrmann does not recognise tone; every later first-hand source (Batibo 1991, Sietsema 1989, Roberts 1992, Matondo 2006, Luhende 2018) treats Sukuma as a tone language with a two-syllable H shift and makes no phonetic word-stress statement, so Herrmann's 'Accent' is best read as an impressionistic mix of H tone and penultimate prominence, not a modern stress analysis. It is the only first-hand statement of word-level prominence placement for Sukuma read in this reading.

sources.citation: Roberts, R. Ruth (1992). A non-metrical theory of Sukuma tone. Ohio State University Working Papers in Linguistics 41: 135-148.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: This paper discusses the tonal system of the Bantu language Sukuma. The interest of Sukuma tone centers around a tone shift whereby a H tone generally shows up two syllables to the right of its underlying location.
sources.locator: pp. 135-148, whole paper; a full-text search for stress/accent full text for stress/accent/penult
sources.note: Tone-shift analysis only (H surfaces two syllables right of its underlying position; argues against Sietsema's 1989 metrical account). The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the text; 'penultimate' appears only in tone-rule contexts (p.143 'a H attached to the penultimate syllable'). No word-stress statement.
